8.title: what your grandmother was actually doing
8.hook: Krishna's poor friend Sudama brings a bundle of rice; why a flower and a cup of water make a whole puja
8.tomorrow: the thing that's yours to do
8.howItsDone: At a home shrine, a devotee may offer water, flowers, incense, a waved lamp and food, ring a bell, and then share the food as prasad; temple priests perform puja in the same spirit on a larger scale.

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma. Your line was what you do, you become. Week two starts at home, with an old friend and a bundle of rice. Day eight.

Two boys once studied under the same teacher: Krishna, a prince, and a poor brahmin boy remembered as Sudama. Years later Krishna is a king in Dwaraka, and Sudama's family is going hungry. His wife begs him: go and see your old friend. He has nothing to bring, so she begs four handfuls of flattened rice from the neighbors, and he ties them into his worn cloth. At the palace, Krishna runs to hug him, washes his feet, and seats him on his own bed. Then he asks: what did you bring me? Sudama is too ashamed to hand over cheap rice. So Krishna finds it himself, pulls it loose, and eats a handful with joy.
screen: `TWO BOYS, ONE TEACHER.` → `A BUNDLE OF CHEAP RICE.` → `WHAT DID YOU BRING ME?` → `KRISHNA EATS IT WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: This old story holds today's word: puja, the way Hindus worship God with their hands. Before Krishna takes the rice, he says a line many Hindus know by heart, from the Bhagavad Gita: whoever offers me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, with devotion, I accept it. In Sanskrit it begins: patram pushpam phalam toyam. Nothing on that list costs much. What God receives is the devotion, bhakti, the heart tied up in the gift. Now look at a home puja. Many follow the steps of welcoming an honored guest, the way Krishna welcomed Sudama: a seat, water for the feet, water to sip. Then a flower, incense, a waved lamp, a bell, and food. Afterward the food comes back as prasad, a gift from God, shared and eaten. A shrine can be a whole room or one shelf with a picture and a lamp. That's the teaching: in Hinduism, the size of the offering was never the point. A marigold and a cup of water, offered with love, is a whole puja. What you're really bringing is yourself: your care, your attention, for a few minutes given to God. So a grandmother at that shelf before the kettle goes on isn't only keeping a custom. Like Sudama, she's bringing what she has, and it's enough.
screen: `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER` · `THE DEVOTION IS THE GIFT` · `AN HONORED GUEST, THEN PRASAD` · `THE SIZE WAS NEVER THE POINT` · then, large: `ATTENTION IS AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, the smallest puja there is. If you have a shrine or a picture of God, set one thing before it: a flower, a cup of water, a piece of fruit. If you don't, set something you love in front of you. Look at it first. Then offer it with both hands, and give it your full attention. If you pray, say silently: this is for you. If you don't, just let one thing have all of you for a while. The bell holds the time.
Puja. Worship with the hands: water, a flower, a flame, food, offered with devotion. Eighth word.
Your line: attention is an offering. Krishna wanted the rice for the love tied up in it. Give one thing today your whole attention, and you've given what matters. Day eight.

9.title: the thing that's yours to do
9.hook: a warrior puts down his bow and says he no longer knows what's right
9.carry: do the thing that's yours to do
9.howItsDone: Hindus speak of dharma as right action and the order that holds life together, and also of svadharma, one's own duty in a given place and stage of life; the Bhagavad Gita is read and recited as a guide to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: puja. Your line was attention is an offering. Today, the word at the center of the Bhagavad Gita.

The Bhagavad Gita opens on a battlefield. A warrior named Arjuna asks his charioteer to drive him out between the two armies, and he sees his own family on the other side: teachers, uncles, cousins. His bow slips from his hand and he sits down in the chariot. The word he reaches for, to say what he's lost, is today's word.

Dharma gets translated as duty, law or religion, and each of those catches only a piece. It comes from a Sanskrit root meaning to hold, or to support. Dharma is what holds things up: teachers say the dharma of fire is to burn and the dharma of water is to flow. It's what a thing is for, the part it holds in the whole. In the Gita's second chapter, Arjuna says his mind is confused about dharma, and he asks his charioteer, Krishna, to teach him. The rest of the Gita is that teaching. One line from the third chapter shows where it starts: better your own dharma, even done imperfectly, than someone else's done well. Your own dharma is svadharma. So dharma isn't only rules handed down. It's also a question: what is mine to do here? Arjuna isn't missing information. He's lost the thread of what's his to do. That's why Hindus speak of dharma for every stage and role of life: what's mine to hold as a student, as a son or daughter, as a parent, as a friend? Not anyone else's part. Mine.

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, bring to mind one place where you hold something up: a family, a team, a friendship. On the second, ask it as Arjuna did, silently: what's mine to do here? On the third, let the question rest. Arjuna needed the whole Gita to hear his answer; you don't need yours today.
Dharma. From a root meaning to hold: what holds things up, and your share of the holding. Ninth word.
Your line: do the thing that's yours to do. That's dharma: your own part, even done imperfectly. Day nine.

10.title: the one behind your eyes
10.hook: a king's prize of a thousand cows, and a sage asked to point at the self
10.tomorrow: the ocean the wave forgets it is
10.howItsDone: Hindus who follow the Upanishads study the self through teachers and texts, and in meditation and self-inquiry turn attention from thoughts to the one who is aware of them; schools differ on how the self relates to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dharma. Your line was do the thing that's yours to do. Today we turn from what gets done to the one doing it. Day ten.
screen: `DO THE THING THAT'S YOURS TO DO.` → `DAY 10.`

segments.voice: King Janaka once held a great gathering of sages, and set out a thousand cows with gold tied to their horns, a prize for whoever knew the most about the highest truth. Nobody dared claim them. Then the sage Yajnavalkya calmly told his student: drive them home. The other sages were furious, and one by one they stood up to test him. One, a man named Ushasta, pressed him on a single point: show me this self you speak of. Plainly. The way you'd point and say: that's a cow, that's a horse. Today's word is what he was asking to see.
screen: `A THOUSAND COWS, GOLD ON THEIR HORNS.` → `DRIVE THEM HOME.` → `SHOW ME THE SELF. PLAINLY.`

segments.voice: Atman. The self. Not the self in selfie, the personality you show the world. The Upanishads use atman for the deepest you: the one that is aware. Yajnavalkya's answer turns Ushasta's question around: you can't see the seer of seeing. You can't hear the hearer of hearing. The one who looks can't become one more thing on the table to be looked at. Elsewhere the same Upanishad describes the self by saying what it is not: neti, neti. Not this, not this. Whatever you can point to, the body, the breath, the busy mind, the self is not that. This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: you are not only your body, your moods or your story. Hindu scripture teaches that the atman isn't born and doesn't die; bodies change around it, even life after life. That's why, at a funeral, a Hindu family may say the one they loved hasn't simply ended: the body is set down, and the self goes on. Hindu schools describe the atman in different ways. Some teach that the self is one with the whole. Others teach that it is a distinct soul, forever dear to God and dependent on God. Tomorrow brings the word for the whole. And the turn is practical. When worry comes, it comes as something seen: a thought, a tight chest, a story about tomorrow. The Upanishad points past all of it, to the one who sees, the part of you no bad day can touch.
screen: `ATMAN — THE SELF THAT IS AWARE` · `NETI, NETI — NOT THIS, NOT THIS` · `NOT BORN, DOESN'T DIE` · `SCHOOLS DESCRIBE IT DIFFERENTLY` · then, large: `SOMEONE IS IN THERE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to notice the noticer. Let your eyes close or soften. Let a thought arrive, any thought. Don't follow it. Just see that it's there. Now notice that something saw it. Rest there for a moment, not in the thought, in the seeing. Another thought will come; that's what thoughts do. Same move: see it, then notice the one who saw. No need to get anywhere. The bell holds the time.
Atman. The self: not the body, not the thoughts, but the one aware of them. Tenth word.
Your line: someone is in there. That's the atman. When worry shows up today, ask once, quietly: who is seeing this? Day ten.

screen: `DAY 10 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE OCEAN THE WAVE FORGETS IT IS.`

11.title: the ocean the wave forgets it is
11.hook: a proud son, a lump of salt in water, and the whole that's in every sip
11.tomorrow: anyone who turns a light on
11.howItsDone: Hindus study the Upanishads' teaching on Brahman with teachers and commentaries, and the schools of Vedanta (Shankara's Advaita, Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita, Madhva's Dvaita) each read 'tat tvam asi' in their own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday: atman, the one behind your eyes. Your line was someone is in there. Did you catch yourself watching a thought? Today the word gets bigger, so we'll go slow. Day eleven.

A young man comes home after twelve years of study, very sure of himself. His father, Uddalaka, asks him one question he can't answer, and starts teaching him again. One day he hands him a lump of salt: put this in a cup of water, and come back in the morning. The son, Shvetaketu, does. Next morning the father says: bring me the salt. The boy looks. It's gone. Sip from the top, says the father. Salty. From the middle. Salty. From the bottom. Salty. The salt is in every sip, and he can't find it anywhere. The story is told in the Chandogya Upanishad, and it points at today's word, a big one.
screen: `HOME AFTER TWELVE YEARS, SURE OF HIMSELF.` → `A LUMP OF SALT. A CUP OF WATER.` → `IT'S IN EVERY SIP.`

segments.voice: Brahman. Not Brahma, the creator god in the stories, and not Brahmin, the priestly class. Different words. Brahman is the name the Upanishads give to the whole: the reality underneath everything, what everything comes from and returns to. Like the salt, it isn't one more thing you can pick out. It's in every taste. The same chapter of the Chandogya has another picture. Rivers flow, some east, some west, and in the end they reach the sea and become the sea. And once there, the Upanishad says, they don't know: I am this river, I am that one. Now the line the father keeps saying to his son, again and again in that chapter: tat tvam asi. That's what you are. Yesterday's word, atman, the self, and today's word, Brahman, the whole: the Upanishad brings them face to face. Hindu thinkers read the line in more than one way. Advaita Vedanta, taught by Shankara, reads it as identity: the self and the whole are not two. Ramanuja's school reads it as one whole with real differences inside it, the self living in God and God as the self's inner ruler. Madhva's school keeps the self and God distinct, the self always dependent on God. These readings sit side by side in the tradition, and nobody here has to choose. Just notice what the picture does. In the Upanishad, the rivers don't dry up somewhere along the way. They become the sea. And today's title borrows the picture for one way of hearing it: a wave that is ocean the whole time, even while it forgets. And it's one root of things you'll see in Hindu life: bowing to a river, honoring a guest, greeting someone with folded hands. For many Hindus, the same reality is in all of it.
screen: `BRAHMAN — THE WHOLE` · `SALT IN WATER, RIVERS IN THE SEA` · `TAT TVAM ASI — THAT'S WHAT YOU ARE` · `READ MORE THAN ONE WAY` · then, large: `NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the river reach the sea. Sit and breathe. Bring a river to mind, any one you've seen or can imagine. Let it carry this life, this name, today's worries. Follow it as it moves. Then let it reach the sea, and let the edges go. Not lost: arrived. Rest there, in the big water. Some rest there with one name of God in mind. The bell holds the time.
Brahman. The whole, the reality under everything. Not Brahma, not Brahmin. Eleventh word.
Your line: not two. The salt is in every sip. When someone feels far from you today, remember what the Upanishad says is in them too. Day eleven.

screen: `DAY 11 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ANYONE WHO TURNS A LIGHT ON.`

12.title: anyone who turns a light on
12.hook: a boy tells the truth at a teacher's door; why Hindus honor the guru
12.howItsDone: Hindus may learn from a guru within a lineage (parampara), receive instruction or a mantra from them, and honor teachers on Guru Purnima; in some traditions, God is understood as the first or inner guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Brahman. Your line was not two. Today, a boy who told the truth at a teacher's door, and the teacher who took him in. Day twelve.

A boy named Satyakama wants to study with a teacher, and a student was expected to name his family line. So he asks his mother. She tells him the truth: when she was young she worked as a servant, going from place to place, and she doesn't know his line. All she knows is that her name is Jabala and his is Satyakama. So he walks to the teacher Gautama and repeats it, word for word. The teacher's answer: only a true brahmin would speak like that. Go and fetch the firewood. I'll teach you, because you didn't stray from the truth.
screen: `WHAT'S OUR FAMILY LINE?` → `SHE TELLS HIM THE TRUTH.` → `SO DOES HE.` → `FETCH THE FIREWOOD.`

segments.voice: Guru. A teacher, but in Hinduism much more than a teacher of facts: the one who helps you see. A later text plays with the sound: gu is darkness, and ru is what removes it. Wordplay, but a vivid one. Watch what Satyakama's teacher does next. He hands the boy four hundred thin, weak cows to look after, and Satyakama says he won't come back until they're a thousand. Years pass in the forest. On the way home he's taught by a bull, a fire, a swan and a diving bird. He arrives glowing, and his teacher says: your face shines like someone who knows. But Satyakama asks him to teach him anyway. Learning that comes from a teacher, he says, is the kind that turns out best. That's how Hinduism holds the guru: not a salesman with a course, but the one who lifts the dark. An old charge to students says it plainly: treat your mother as God, your father as God, your teacher as God. It's why many students of Indian music and dance touch their teacher's feet before they perform, why learning passes down a long line of teachers, and why, on the full moon called Guru Purnima, students thank their gurus. For some Hindus, God is the first guru, or the guru within. Either way, the light came from somewhere.
screen: `GU — DARKNESS, RU — WHAT REMOVES IT` · `400 COWS, YEARS IN THE FOREST` · `LEARNING FROM A TEACHER` · `TREAT YOUR TEACHER AS GOD` · then, large: `THANK A TEACHER TODAY.`

segments.voice: Today, remember one light. Rest your hands in your lap, or bring your palms together the way students greet a teacher. Bring to mind one person who helped you see: a teacher, a grandparent, a coach, a friend with one true sentence. Let their face come. Then, silently, thank them. If you pray, thank God for them too. If you like, bow your head a little, the way a student does. The bell holds the time.
Guru. A teacher who helps you see; in one Upanishad's play on the sound, the one who removes the dark. Twelfth word.
Your line: thank a teacher today. In Hinduism a guru is honored almost like God; a two-line message to yours is a good start. Day twelve.

13.title: why 108
13.hook: a boy pushed off his father's lap, a sage's mantra, and the beads that count it
13.carry: count what you want to keep
13.howItsDone: Devotees do japa with a mala, moving one bead per repetition of a mantra or a divine name, often at a set time each day; some count on the sections of the fingers instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: guru. Your line was thank a teacher today. Today a sage acts as one, and gives a small boy a mantra. Day thirteen.

A little prince named Dhruva tries to climb onto his father the king's lap, and his stepmother stops him. Only her son sits there, she says. If you want that seat, go and pray to God. Dhruva runs to his own mother, Suniti, in tears. She doesn't fight back. She tells him: she's right about one thing. Turn to God. So the small boy walks into the forest. On the way he meets the sage Narada, who tries to send him home. When Dhruva won't go, Narada gives him a mantra: om namo bhagavate vasudevaya, a bow to the Lord. Dhruva sits by the river Yamuna and says it, again, and again, and again.
screen: `PULLED OFF HIS FATHER'S LAP.` → `THEN TURN TO GOD.` → `A MANTRA FROM NARADA.` → `AGAIN, AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Japa. Repeating a mantra, or a name of God, again and again, often counted. That's what Dhruva does. Month after month he keeps at it, and in the story Vishnu himself comes to the boy. Dhruva is given a kingdom, and in the end a place in the sky that never moves. Hindus call the pole star by his name: Dhruva, the steady one. He got there not by one great prayer, but by one name, said again. In the Gita, Krishna counts that as an offering: among offerings, I am japa. It needs no fire and no flowers. That's why many Hindus receive a mantra from a guru, as Dhruva received his from Narada, and repeat it every day on a mala, a string of beads: one bead, one repetition. By tradition a full mala carries a hundred and eight beads, plus one at the top that the fingers don't pass over. Why a hundred and eight? People give answers from the sky, from lists of divine names, from the body; no text settles it, so we'll leave it open. But a fixed count gives the practice an end. You know when you're done, and you can pick it up again tomorrow. That's how a prayer gets kept: not once, in a crisis, but every day, until it's as steady as the pole star.
screen: `JAPA — A NAME, SAID AGAIN` · `DHRUVA, THE STEADY ONE` · `AMONG OFFERINGS, I AM JAPA` · `108 BEADS, PLUS ONE` · then, large: `COUNT WHAT YOU WANT TO KEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count on your fingers. No beads needed. Each finger has three sections. Touch your thumb to the top section of your index finger: one. The middle section: two. The base: three. Then on to the next finger. With each touch, say om silently on the out-breath, or, if you pray, a name of God you use. Go slowly. You won't reach a hundred and eight today, and Dhruva didn't start there either. The bell holds the time.
Japa. Repeating a mantra or a name, counted, so the hand keeps count and the mind can rest. Thirteenth word.
Your line: count what you want to keep. Dhruva kept one name, again and again. Once today, count a few quiet repetitions on your fingers. Day thirteen.

screen: `DAY 13 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY IT'S SAID THREE TIMES.`

14.title: why it's said three times
14.hook: a teacher and student ask for peace before the lesson: why shanti is said three times
14.howItsDone: Hindu prayers, readings and ceremonies often close with om shanti shanti shanti, the word for peace said three times.

segments.voice: Yesterday: japa. Your line was count what you want to keep. Two weeks today. Today, a word you've probably heard said three times in a row.
screen: `COUNT WHAT YOU WANT TO KEEP.` → `TWO WEEKS.`

segments.voice: In the old forest schools, a lesson didn't begin with the lesson. Teacher and student first said a prayer together, one still chanted today. May we both be protected. May we both be nourished. May we work together with strength. May our study shine. May we never turn against each other. Then they closed it the way many Hindu prayers close: om shanti shanti shanti. Not once. Three times. Traditional teachers read the three as a list.
screen: `TEACHER AND STUDENT, BEFORE THE LESSON.` → `OM SHANTI SHANTI SHANTI.` → `WHY THREE?`

segments.voice: Shanti means peace, the settled kind: calm water with nothing stirring it. The Bhagavad Gita puts it bluntly: for someone without peace, how can there be happiness? Now the three. Traditional teachers read the three shantis as three kinds of trouble, the three places a bad day can come from. Trouble from forces beyond anyone's control: storms, floods, the world. Trouble from other beings: the friend who didn't call, the driver who cut in. And trouble from within: your own body and your own mind. Three sources, three shantis. The teachers add something practical. There's little anyone can do about the first, more about the second, and the third is the one most within reach, and the easiest to skip. So the chant isn't padding. It goes down the list: peace out there, peace between us, peace in here. So when a family ends its prayer this way, or a teacher and student end their chant, they're asking for peace in all three places at once.
screen: `SHANTI — THE SETTLED KIND.` · `THE WORLD.` · `OTHER PEOPLE.` · `YOUR OWN MIND.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell, one shanti on each, said silently. First out-breath: toward the world. Second: toward one person you're not at peace with. You don't have to forgive them. Third: toward your own mind.
Shanti. Peace, the settled kind, said three times: the world, other people, your own mind. Fourteenth word. Puja, dharma, atman, Brahman, guru, japa, shanti: that's week two.
Your line: peace, peace, peace. Next time something rattles you, there are three places it could have come from. Next week brings the doing words. Day fourteen.
